title: Programmable CMOS DAC Operating in Cryogenic Environments for Controlling Superconducting Qubits
authors: A. Pelteku, D. Reitz, M. Covington, A. Frederick, H. Adebayo, K. D. Hillaire, N. Mitran, Z. Steffen, R. Schwartz, Z. Stegen, J. X. Przybysz, J. Yager, C. Walter, T. Graves, D. Meyer, J. Clark, G. R. Boyd, A. Pesetski
abstract: This paper presents the design and test results of a CMOS current-based Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) that operates at cryogenic temperatures and that can be used to precisely control the amount of flux coupled to qubits or that can be used in the readout of superconducting circuits. The current pulse output can be controlled in terms of its amplitude, rise and fall slopes, via digital controls, and pulse width, via external triggers, while driving a superconducting circuit. The design has been implemented in a planar 90 nm CMOS process and test results closely match circuit predictions. The solution's wide degree of digital tunability affords potential application of the same device to many types of quantum circuits, beyond those discussed here. Due to the wide-ranging flexibility of digital CMOS control, we envision that this DAC design will enable the next generation of high-fidelity cryo-CMOS control architectures for superconducting qubits.
summary: This paper details the design, testing, and validation of a programmable CMOS Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) engineered to operate in cryogenic environments. This DAC allows for the precise, digitally controlled injection of current pulses to manipulate the magnetic flux of superconducting qubits. The successful demonstration proves a key component for building scalable, high-fidelity control electronics for quantum computation.
main_problem: The core problem is developing a high-fidelity, programmable Digital to Analog Converter (DAC) capable of operating at cryogenic temperatures to precisely control the magnetic flux coupled to superconducting qubits.
main_result: The designed CMOS DAC successfully demonstrated tunable analog current control at cryogenic temperatures, showing potential for enabling next-generation, high-fidelity cryo-CMOS control architectures for superconducting qubits.
method: The authors designed and tested a CMOS current-based DAC, utilizing digital controls (FSMs, SPI interfaces) and a novel pre-charge circuit to generate precise, programmable current pulses.
model_or_system: The system involves a planar 90nm CMOS ASIC interfacing with superconducting qubits (like Transmon or flux qubits) via current-return 50 Ohm lines. The control mechanism relies on injecting precisely controlled current pulses to manipulate the qubit's flux state.
key_observables: Qubit preparation and readout fidelity, control waveform characteristics (amplitude, rise/fall slopes, slew rate), and output current amplitude/pulse width.
important_parameters: Operating temperatures (down to 600 mK), DAC output current range ($\approx 130 \mu	ext{A}$ to $403 \mu	ext{A}$), and achievable start delays ($	au < 20 	ext{ ns}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that low-pass filtering can mitigate control noise effects, and future work must address thermal management and packaging for scaling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the DAC's block diagram, the pre-charge circuit, and experimental results showing tunable pulse amplitude and width at both room temperature and 600 mK, confirming consistency across multiplexed states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from the scientific need (precise cryogenic control) to the detailed design (CMOS architecture, pre-charge circuit), followed by simulation results demonstrating tunability, and finally, experimental validation at cryogenic temperatures.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the classical control bottleneck in superconducting quantum computing, providing a tangible, scalable electronic solution for manipulating quantum states.

figures.caption: Figure 1 – The application of this fast IDAC. R0 is a superconducting qubit. DC controls are applied to bias the QFPs near its operating point, and a fast flux pulse provided by this DAC controls its operation.

Figure 3 – CMOS DAC iteration 1 readout fidelity when there is nominal R = 50 Ω, T = 1 K thermal noise on the CMOS DAC control line (red), and when there is a low-pass filter attached to the output (green, blue). The low-pass cutoff frequency is swept on the x-axis, showing that the fidelity returns to its noise- free value once the noise PSD at frequencies above the minimum, relevant quantum transition frequency is filtered out.

Figure 4 – Functional Depiction of the Current Pulse, showing ideal operation of the device. An initial “start” signal is sent to the device, which begins its output current ramp up after some time τ. The output current ramps down some time τ after receiving a “stop” signal.

Figure 5 – Overall block diagram of the CMOS current DAC. Here the external trigger signal refers more generically to both the start and stop triggers that are used for initiating the start and stop of the output current waveform.
Figure 6 – Block diagram of Pre-Charge Circuit, demonstrating how capacitor banks are selected by signals from the digital control logic.
